claims.text: NiCoFeCrCu high-entropy alloy can serve as a transition material between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep.
NiCoFeCrCu has a combination of high entropy and lattice distortion that enables this creep-mechanism transition.
The lattice distortion of NiCoFeCrCu can be tailored by changing interface coherency in HEA multilayers.
The high entropy of NiCoFeCrCu causes significant lattice distortion.
Lattice distortion affects dislocation mobility in NiCoFeCrCu.
Lattice distortion affects atomic diffusion in NiCoFeCrCu.
Increasing interface coherency decreases the lattice mismatch between adjacent layers.
Decreasing lattice mismatch reduces stress concentration at the interfaces.
Reduced interfacial stress concentration lowers the driving force for dislocation glide.
Increasing interface coherency promotes a transition from diffusion-mediated creep to dislocation-mediated creep.
The initial NiCoFeCrCu alloy is polycrystalline with an average grain size of 10 micrometers.
Controlled sputtering conditions and substrate temperatures can produce NiCoFeCrCu multilayers with varying interface coherency.
The proposed creep conditions are 800 degrees Celsius and 500 MPa for 100 hours.
Interface coherency is measured through the degree of lattice mismatch between adjacent layers.
Creep under the proposed conditions involves thermally activated dislocation glide and diffusion-mediated creep.
A high-coherency NiCoFeCrCu multilayer will have a steady-state creep rate of 6.0 × 10^-5 s^-1.
The predicted rate is 40% lower than the baseline rate of 1.0 × 10^-4 s^-1 for a low-coherency NiCoFeCrCu multilayer.
An interface-coherency value above 0.8 is the critical boundary for the creep-mechanism transition.
Previous studies on lattice mismatch in HEA multilayers support the interface-coherency threshold of 0.8.
The hypothesis is falsified if high interface coherency does not reduce steady-state creep rate by at least 25% relative to the low-coherency control.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis states that greater coherency lowers the driving force for dislocation glide while simultaneously claiming that it promotes a transition toward dislocation-mediated creep. Without an additional rate-controlling explanation, the asserted mechanistic direction is internally inconsistent.
